headline: Cape May Rips: C-Minus for Stripers, A for Blues, Weakfish Doing Their Job at Dusk
subhead: Warm water has pushed the bass deep and nocturnal, but a fresh wave of bluefish and a reliable dusk weakfish bite are carrying the two-bay game this week.
body_markdown:
Rips grade this week: C-minus on stripers, straight A on blues, B-plus on fluke if you know where to look, and an incomplete on drum because that ship sailed back in May. That's the honest read, and I'm not going to dress it up.

Here's why. Water off Cape May Point and through the rips has been sitting warm — mid-70s and holding — and that's shoved the bass down and put them on a nighttime clock. I've had two charters this week work the outgoing tide through the rips at first light, working 20 to 40 feet with white bucktails tipped with a strip of Gulp, and we picked at fish, nothing you'd write home about. Two shorts, one 29-incher that went back, and a lot of quiet rod holders. That's what warm water does to a striper — they'll feed, but they do it after the sun goes down or right at first light when the thermal layer's thinnest. If you want bass right now, fish the last hour of dark into sunrise on the outgoing, bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig soaking bottom in that 25 to 35 foot band off the Point. Anything past 8 a.m. and you're mostly wasting bait.

What's not slow is the bluefish. There's a fresh wave pushing down the coast right now, and it's showing up hard in the rips and right at the mouth of Hereford Inlet. These aren't dink blues either — mixed sizes with some genuine choppers in the 4 to 6 pound class hitting bunker spoons and diamond jigs worked fast through the current seams. If you're marking bait getting worked over on the sounder near the Inlet jetty on a moving tide, don't overthink it — toss a Hopkins or a Kastmaster and hang on. This has been the most consistent action of the week, hands down.

Fluke are holding up their end, and we flagged this last week — said the bite would stay steady rather than blitz-level, with keepers mixed in among the shorts on structure-oriented drifts, and that's exactly what's playing out. Hereford Inlet channel edges near the Coast Guard station, 15 to 25 feet, drifting on the last of the flood into the top of the ebb, white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail is putting keepers in the cooler along with plenty of shorts you're throwing back. We also called the reef bite softening as the shallow bay water climbed — that's held true too. The inshore reef sites right off the Cape aren't producing like they were three weeks ago; the fluke have slid to deeper structure and toward the mouth of the bay where there's more exchange and cooler bottom water. If you're running out to the reef, fish it deep and don't waste time on the shallow edges — that pattern's played out for now. Triggerfish are showing up as a nice surprise on those same deeper wrecks, hitting small chunks of clam on a simple bottom rig. Nothing to target specifically, but a fun bonus when the fluke bite is slow between drifts.

Over on the Delaware Bay side, the drum run wrapped up back in May like it always does — if you're asking about black drum in August, I'll save you the trip, they're gone until next spring. But weakfish have been doing quiet, honest work, and this is the other call we made last week that's holding: the bay bite has stayed a low-light, current-driven program, with weakfish and flounder showing best on moving tide at dawn and dusk. Fortescue and the mouth of the bay have been the sweet spots — 12 to 18 feet, Gulp shrimp on a light jighead or a bucktail tipped with a shedder crab strip, fished right on the bottom as the tide starts to move. Midday, when the sun's high and the water's dead calm, forget it — I've had charters sit on marked fish for two hours at noon and get nothing, then watch the rods bend the second the tide broke at 6 p.m. That's the pattern right now, and it's not changing until the water cools.

Looking ahead, we're building toward the new moon and the tides are going to get some teeth back in the next few days. Stronger current usually means a better shot at the rips holding fish through more of the tide cycle instead of just the dawn window, so if I had one day to fish this weekend, I'd take the pre-dawn outgoing at the Point and stay through the first hour of light, then run over to Hereford for fluke on the back half of the flood. Keep an eye on the sky too — any afternoon thunderstorms rolling off the mainland can muddy up the bay fast and shut the weakfish sight-bite down for a tide or two. If that happens, give it a day to clear before you make the run to Fortescue. Otherwise, this pattern's stable enough to plan around — just don't expect the bass to cooperate until nights get longer or a real cold front finally shows up.
